A large regional conglomerate with multi-currency debt faced mismatched interest-rate exposures between USD and AED, creating earnings volatility as global rates rose.

We structured a five-year USD 1bn to AED cross-currency swap to convert the client's USD floating-rate liabilities into AED-denominated cash flows. The swap aligned both currencies' interest benchmarks and synchronised payment cycles.

The client achieved full rate and currency alignment, reduced P&L volatility, and gained predictable funding costs for long-term capital projects, strengthening their credit profile and building investor confidence.
Removing FX risk from foreign-currency debt
A corporate borrower's USD loan exposed repayments to currency movements, adding uncertainty to its debt-service costs.
We structured an AED 2bn USD/AED cross-currency swap, converting the exposure into a local-currency position with flexible settlement timing and call options for early unwinding.
The client removed currency risk from its debt portfolio and now manages liquidity entirely in dirhams, sharpening financial planning and return calculations on new investments.
Oil hedge for an aviation client
A leading Middle-Eastern airline faced jet-fuel price volatility, threatening operational budgets and long-term route planning as energy markets fluctuated sharply.

We structured a multi-year jet-fuel hedging programme using swaps and zero-cost option collars, tailored to the airline's fuel consumption profile and accounting needs. Our commodities desk actively monitored market spreads and adjusted strike levels to maintain budget discipline while taking advantage of favourable price movements.

Our hedging programme stabilised fuel costs over multiple years, strengthened earnings predictability, and protected competitive ticket pricing. The airline preserved profit margins through double-digit oil volatility.

Ijarah provides medium- and long-term financing for capital assets by allowing you to lease equipment, machinery, or vehicles without large upfront payments. We purchase the asset you select, lease it to you for an agreed term, and transfer ownership once payments are complete.
Structured asset leasing, where Emirates NBD purchases the asset on your behalf and leases it to you over an agreed period, with ownership transferring to you once all payments are completed.
Suitable for durable assets that remain intact through use, such as equipment, vehicles, and other non-consumable capital goods.

Forward Ijarah enables you to finance assets under construction through a Shariah-compliant structure that links a future sale with a forward lease. We fund the developer during production, and once the asset is completed it is leased back to you under an agreed payment plan, providing certainty throughout the process.
Medium- to long-term financing structures primarily for construction of infrastructure projects including homes, offices, and plants.
The completed asset is leased to you for a specific period; upon lease completion, asset ownership is transferred to you.
Lease amounts must be known on the contract date.
Provides flexibility, as payments can be made in installments linked to project completion.
Emirates NBD undertakes to pay the contracted developer or builder in full, or in specific stages.

Murabaha is a sale-based financing structure in which Emirates NBD purchases a specified asset at your request, assuming ownership risk and then sells it to you at a disclosed cost-plus-profit on a deferred payment basis, providing transparent, Shariah-compliant financing without conventional lending.
Suitable for businesses of all sizes, from SMEs to large corporates.
An effective way to purchase a wide range of eligible assets, including raw materials, semi-finished and finished goods, or store and spare requirements.

Musharaka is a partnership structure where both Emirates NBD and the client contribute capital, share profits per agreed ratios, and absorb losses in line with the original investment contribution. Depending on the financing required, Emirates NBD would become a partner in your business or a defined segment, underpinned by strong governance and clear performance-monitoring.
Once all partners contribute capital to the joint pool, the Musharaka's assets become jointly owned.
Each partner may participate in managing the business.
Losses are shared by all partners in proportion to their invested capital.

Meet your liquidity needs, even without business assets, through Shariah-compliant monetisation. Tawarruq offers a flexible way to access working capital and longer-term financing. Emirates NBD would purchase commodities from a supplier and sell them on to you, so that you can generate the liquidity you need by selling those commodities on to another party.
Meets all types of Shariah-compliant financing needs.

Wakala is an agency arrangement where Emirates NBD appoints the client to execute agreed Shariah-compliant investments to generate expected returns. Profits are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio, with the wakil managing the investments on the bank's behalf and retaining any excess return as an added incentive.
Profit is allocated based on the agreed ratio.
Expected returns are outlined by the bank.
The client executes the investment to realise those returns.

Mudaraba Finance is a partnering arrangement where Emirates NBD, as Rab Al Mal, supplies capital to a business or Mudarib, to invest in a defined commercial venture. Profits are shared under an agreed ratio, with losses absorbed by the bank unless the client is negligent, engages in misconduct, or commits fraud.
Used for term finance and working capital needs.
Provides flexibility in terms of utilization of funds and terms.

An Islamic Fixed Deposit is a Shariah-compliant way to place your funds for a set period. Your money is invested in approved assets and you receive profit based on the performance of those investments, following structures such as Mudaraba or Wakala. No interest is paid at any point, and all activity is overseen by the bank’s Internal Shariah Supervision Committee.
<1>What are the types of Islamic Deposits offered by Emirates NBD Islamic?</1> <3><4/></3>

Emirates NBD Islamic offers two main types of deposits. Mudaraba deposits work on a profit-sharing basis where the bank manages your funds in Shariah-compliant investments. Wakala deposits work through an agency arrangement where the bank invests your funds on your behalf with an expected profit rate. Both options follow Shariah guidelines and differ mainly in how profit is calculated.
<1>How can I open an Islamic Fixed Deposit?</1> <3><4/></3>

You can open an Islamic Fixed Deposit once you have an active account with Emirates NBD Islamic. The process can be completed through a branch or using the bank’s digital channels. You choose the amount, the currency and the term, then review and sign the Shariah-compliant contract. After the bank confirms your request, the funds are placed for the agreed period.
<1>What is the minimum amount required for opening an Islamic Fixed Deposit?</1> <3><4/></3>

The minimum amount depends on the type of deposit you choose. Mudaraba deposits usually start from AED 10,000 or the equivalent in USD. Wakala deposits are designed for larger placements and start from AED 4mn or USD 1mn. These thresholds may vary and should be confirmed with the bank at the time of application.
<1>Can I open an Islamic Fixed Deposit in different currencies?</1> <3><4/></3>

Yes, Islamic Fixed Deposits are generally available in AED and USD. Availability may vary depending on the specific deposit structure you choose. If you require another currency, you can check with the bank to confirm whether it is currently offered under a Shariah-compliant structure.

Explore key fraud risks affecting corporates in the UAE and GCC, including phishing, invoice fraud, BEC, cyberattacks and payment redirection. Learn how to safeguard your treasury operations and protect digital banking activity with clear controls and governance steps.
<1>What is phishing and how can you recognise it?</1> <3><4/></3>

Phishing occurs when attackers impersonate a trusted party to obtain your credentials, payment details or confidential information. Warning signs include urgent requests for login details, unusual sender addresses, and suspicious links or attachments. Always validate unexpected instructions through an independent channel before acting.
<1>What is invoice fraud and how can you prevent it?</1> <3><4/></3>

Invoice fraud uses fake, altered or duplicated invoices, often mimicking a genuine vendor, to trick you into paying a criminal. Reduce exposure by matching each invoice to a purchase order, scrutinising any change to a supplier's payment details, and applying maker-checker controls for beneficiary updates. A brief verification step protects high-value transactions.
<1>What is Business Email Compromise (BEC) and how can you defend against it?</1> <3><4/></3>

BEC involves fraudulent or compromised email accounts used to request urgent payments or sensitive data from your team. Strengthen protection by confirming unusual or high-value instructions through a phone call, enabling dual approval for payments, and using strong authentication with regular access reviews. If an email feels out of pattern, pause and verify.
<1>What are insider threats and how can your company mitigate them?</1> <3><4/></3>

Insider threats arise when employees or contractors misuse access to manipulate data, divert funds or leak information. Mitigation includes restricting permissions to essential roles, using dual control for financial approvals, reviewing access rights regularly, and maintaining clear reporting channels for concerns. Controls and transparency reduce internal risk.
<1>What types of cyberattacks target businesses, and how can you protect your organisation?</1> <3><4/></3>

Ransomware, malware, credential theft and unauthorised access increasingly target corporate digital banking environments. Strengthen your defences by keeping systems and patches current, training employees to identify suspicious activity, enforcing strong authentication, and monitoring digital banking activity daily. Preparedness limits financial and operational impact.
<1>How can you protect your business when using Emirates NBD digital channels?</1> <3><4/></3>

When using businessONLINE, smartTRADE, smartSCF or Emirates NBD Pay, access platforms only through official URLs, review payment details before approval, apply role-based access, disable inactive users, and enable two-factor authentication. Avoid approving transactions over public Wi-Fi. Strong internal governance is your most effective safeguard.
<1>How can you avoid supplier or payment redirection fraud?</1> <3><4/></3>

Redirection fraud targets an existing supplier relationship: criminals quietly switch a trusted beneficiary's bank details to an account they control. Protect your payment flows by maintaining whitelisted beneficiaries, limiting who can amend bank details, and callback-verifying every change through a pre-agreed contact. Treat last-minute or urgent amendment requests as high-risk and verify before releasing funds.
<1>What should you do if you suspect or experience a fraud incident?</1> <3><4/></3>

Act immediately. Contact Emirates NBD Corporate Fraud Support on 600 54 0000. Pause approvals, block suspicious access, and preserve evidence such as emails, logs, invoices and screenshots. Alert your internal IT or security teams and notify regulators or authorities where required. Rapid escalation improves the likelihood of recovery.

Fraud tactics grow more convincing every day, and businesses are a prime target. Recognising the warning signs early is what stops an attack before it lands. The guidance and tools on this page help your teams act with confidence and keep fraud from costing you.
Today's scams blend technology and social engineering, and they are built to slip past a busy team. When something feels off, do not engage. Here are the tactics to watch for.
Urgent calls, WhatsApp or SMS messages push you to act fast, demanding you click a link, add a beneficiary, or share details. Pause, verify the source through official channels, then act.
Fraudsters use false offers, rebates, or reward programmes to compromise corporate data. Always verify the legitimacy of the offer before engaging.

Fraudulent sites and payment links convincingly imitate trusted vendors to harvest credentials. Always verify URLs, do not click on unknown links, and use official portals or approved channels for payments.

Scammers alter payment details, such as mismatched IBANs or verification requests, to divert funds away from your intended destination. Always verify account name and IBAN via a known contact before making transfers.
Keep one-time codes private and never share them. Any request for an OTP, password, or SmartPass approval is a red flag. Emirates NBD will never ask you for them.
